description: A home cook and allotment gardener's shelf mixing fermentation, growing and seasonal cooking pieces against incidental everyday words (car, phone, weekend, neighbour, morning, box) that a naive word counter might mistake for topics.
profile: A home cook and allotment gardener who reads about fermentation, growing vegetables and seasonal cooking.

articles.title: Keeping a Sourdough Starter Alive
articles.gist: A diary-style piece on the daily ritual of feeding a sourdough starter and why slow fermentation makes better bread.
articles.text:
I keep my sourdough starter on the counter, and every morning I lift the cloth and check the fermentation underneath before I have even made tea. The morning ritual barely changes: a spoonful of flour, a spoonful of water, and a look for the small dome of bubbles that tells me the fermentation is doing its work. Some mornings the starter is sluggish, and other mornings it has doubled overnight, because sourdough is famously moody about temperature.

I started this jar of sourdough two winters ago, coaxed from a handful of rye flour and a week of patient morning feedings. I still photograph the starter most mornings on my phone, a habit that began as a way to track fermentation and turned into something closer to a diary. Scrolling back through the phone now, I can watch the sourdough rise and fall across two years of mornings, a strange kind of time-lapse kept entirely on a phone I otherwise use for nothing more interesting than the weather.

Bread from a good sourdough starter tastes nothing like the loaves I used to buy, and the difference comes down almost entirely to fermentation. A long, slow fermentation breaks down starches that a quick commercial yeast never touches, which is why sourdough sits easier and keeps longer on the counter. A friend once asked, over the fence one morning, whether the sourdough was difficult, and I told her the truth: it is not difficult, it is only slow, and slowness is the whole point of fermentation.

These days the reminder I set on my phone for feeding time is almost unnecessary, because the smell of the starter tells me when the fermentation has run its course. I still glance at the phone on baking mornings, though, mostly to time the proof rather than to check the sourdough itself. By evening the sourdough has usually finished its second rise, and I bake it before bed so the kitchen still smells of fermentation the next morning.

What keeps me coming back to sourdough is not really the bread, good as it is, but the small morning discipline of tending something alive. Fermentation asks for attention rather than effort, and a phone full of morning photographs is proof enough that I have kept giving it exactly that, one ordinary morning at a time.

articles.title: Why Your Sourdough Starter Has Stalled
articles.gist: An explainer diagnosing the common causes of a sluggish sourdough starter and how to restart fermentation.
articles.text:
A sluggish sourdough starter is the single most common complaint I hear, usually arriving as a weekend message from someone who fed their sourdough on Friday and found nothing but a flat, sour puddle by the weekend's end. The good news is that fermentation rarely dies outright; it just slows to a pace that looks, to an impatient eye, like it has stopped.

The first thing to check is temperature. Fermentation is a chemical process, and cold slows it dramatically, so a sourdough starter left in a car overnight, or kept in a chilly hallway, will barely move even when it is perfectly healthy. A cold car is about the worst place for a starter, colder even than a fridge shelf near the door. I once drove a jar of sourdough back from a friend's house in the car on a frosty evening and watched fermentation grind almost to a halt for two days afterwards. If you must transport a starter, wrap the jar in a towel before it goes anywhere near a car boot. Warming the starter to room temperature is usually enough to wake the sourdough back up.

The second cause is a dirty or unbalanced ratio of flour to water. A sourdough starter that is fed too rarely builds up alcohol and acid faster than fermentation can use it, and the culture becomes sluggish in self-defence. Feeding more often, especially over a weekend when you have time to check it twice a day, usually restores a lively sourdough within three or four feeds.

A third, less obvious cause is a change of flour. Fermentation depends on the wild yeast and bacteria already present in the flour and the air, so switching brands can shock a sourdough starter that has adapted to one particular mix. If your weekend baking plans have stalled because the sourdough looks lifeless, try reverting to whatever flour you started with before assuming the fermentation has failed for good.

Finally, do not discard a struggling starter too quickly. I have revived sourdough that looked dead after being left in a cold car boot for a week, simply by feeding it daily for a weekend and watching the fermentation slowly return. Patience, more than any trick, is what nurses a stalled sourdough starter back to full and reliable fermentation.

articles.title: A Baker's Diary: Rye Sourdough in Autumn
articles.gist: A personal essay on baking rye sourdough through autumn and treating fermentation as part of seasonal cooking.
articles.text:
Autumn is when my sourdough habit tightens into something closer to routine, the way seasonal cooking always seems to sharpen once the light starts to go early. I switch from the pale, mild loaves of summer to a darker rye sourdough, heavier with fermentation and better suited to soup than to salad, which feels like the right kind of seasonal cooking for the month.

My neighbour, who keeps chickens two gardens over, has taken to leaving a note on my gate when she wants a loaf, and I have taken to leaving one on hers when the rye sourdough comes out heavier than usual. It has become a small, wordless exchange that only really works because sourdough keeps so well; a loaf handed to a neighbour on Monday is still good by the neighbour's Thursday, which is more than can be said for most seasonal cooking.

Rye flour ferments differently to wheat, and the fermentation smells sharper, almost like the vinegar you use for seasonal cooking with pickled autumn vegetables. I have learned to trust that sharper smell rather than fight it, because a rye sourdough that smells mild has usually been under-fermented, and the fermentation needs another few hours before shaping. My neighbour says she can smell when I am baking from her own kitchen, which either means my fermentation is working or my extractor fan needs replacing.

What I like about folding sourdough into seasonal cooking is that it refuses to be rushed by the calendar the way so much autumn cooking is. Fermentation runs on its own clock, cool and slow as the season itself, and a rye sourdough left overnight in an unheated kitchen behaves almost exactly as the month behaves: patient, a little stubborn, and better for the wait. By the time my neighbour and I have swapped four or five loaves, the fermentation smell has become as much a marker of the season as fallen leaves, and the rye sourdough itself has become my clearest expression of seasonal cooking all year.

articles.title: Two Kimchi Recipes for a Small Kitchen
articles.gist: A practical how-to comparing a quick and a slow method for making kimchi at home.
articles.text:
Kimchi rewards patience more than precision, which is good news for anyone making it in a small kitchen on a weekday morning before work. I make two versions in rotation: a quick kimchi that is ready to eat within a morning and a half, and a slower kimchi that spends a full week fermenting on the counter before it goes into the fridge.

The quick kimchi starts the night before, when I salt the cabbage and leave it to soften overnight, so that by morning it is limp enough to mix with the chilli paste, garlic and fish sauce. This version of kimchi is barely fermented at all by the time it is eaten, closer to a spicy salad than to true kimchi, but it satisfies the craving on a morning when a full batch would take too long.

The slow kimchi is the one I actually plan my mornings around. I mix it on a Saturday morning, pack it tightly into a jar, and check it every morning after that, pressing the cabbage back under its own brine so mould has nowhere to start. By the fourth or fifth morning the kimchi has turned properly sour, and I put a spoonful in a small bowl before breakfast most mornings just to track how the kimchi is developing. I set a phone timer for the fourth day, though I usually check the jar before it goes off.

I photograph the jar most mornings, too, not because a picture of kimchi is interesting but because the colour changes are the clearest sign of how the batch is progressing, and I sometimes send the photo from my phone to a friend who is also making kimchi that week. She replies most mornings with her own phone photo, so we end up trading kimchi progress reports over a screen instead of a fence. I check the phone clock more than the actual time some mornings, just to log when each stage started, and the phone gallery is now mostly kimchi, which says something about my mornings.

By the second week, both jars of kimchi have found their balance, and I fold the sourer batch into rice or noodles most mornings, saving the milder one for guests who find real kimchi a little startling. Whichever kimchi I am eating, the habit of checking a jar every morning has become the small, reliable structure around which the rest of my cooking day gets built.

articles.title: The Many Regional Faces of Kimchi
articles.gist: An essay surveying how kimchi varies by region and season across Korea, and why it belongs to seasonal cooking.
articles.text:
Kimchi is often described in the singular, as though one recipe covers it, but travel across Korea and you find a different kimchi in almost every province, each shaped by climate and by what seasonal cooking demanded of a particular harvest. Coastal kimchi tends to lean on seafood brines, while mountain kimchi is often milder, built around whatever vegetables seasonal cooking made available before refrigeration existed at all.

The most striking regional kimchi I have made at home is a watery, radish-based version meant to be eaten as a cold soup, which upends most people's idea of what kimchi even is. It belongs to winter seasonal cooking specifically, developed in regions where a jar of kimchi needed to provide both food and liquid through months when little else was growing. Packing a whole cabbage into a storage box for months, the way households once did before jars became common, is itself a piece of seasonal cooking history worth remembering.

Other regions favour a drier kimchi, packed loosely into an earthenware box and left to ferment underground, where the temperature stays steadier than any kitchen counter. This underground approach turns kimchi-making into genuine seasonal cooking infrastructure rather than a single afternoon's project, something closer to how a root cellar works for potatoes. Even now, some kitchens keep a dedicated box or crock for exactly this purpose, treated with the same seriousness as any other tool of seasonal cooking.

What ties every regional kimchi together, despite the different vegetables and different timings, is the underlying logic of seasonal cooking: preserve the harvest you have, using salt and time rather than heat, so that a version of summer's abundance survives into a leaner season. My phone is full of photographs from a single trip through three regions, each kimchi tasting distinctly of its own place, packed into its own kind of box, following its own local rhythm of seasonal cooking that predates any single recipe I could write down. I photographed each version on my phone as I went, comparing the colours side by side later that evening, and the phone folder from that trip has grown into something like a small archive of kimchi. Whenever I want to remember a particular brine, I scroll back through the same phone folder, and a friend messaged my phone last week asking about the radish version, so I sent her three photos straight from the trip. I still have one of those storage boxes at home, though I use it for onions rather than cabbage now, and a second box of the same kind sits empty in the shed waiting for next year's cabbages.

articles.title: A Fermenting Weekend: Kimchi and Kombucha Together
articles.gist: A light blog post about spending a weekend making kimchi alongside a batch of kombucha.
articles.text:
Some weekends are for the allotment and some weekends are entirely given over to jars, and this last weekend was firmly the second kind. I had promised myself a kimchi weekend months ago, and I finally cleared a Saturday and most of a Sunday to make two big jars of kimchi and, almost as an afterthought, a batch of kombucha using the culture a friend had handed over the weekend before.

The kimchi came first, because it needed the cabbage salted overnight before the rest of the weekend's work could start. I drove to the market early on the Saturday, mostly because the car was already loaded with empty jars for a friend, and came home with more napa cabbage than any sensible kimchi recipe requires. By the time the kimchi was packed away, the car smelled faintly of garlic for the rest of the weekend.

Kombucha, by contrast, is almost embarrassingly easy once you have a starter culture, and it felt like the lazier half of the weekend's work. I brewed the sweet tea, let it cool in the back of the car on the drive home from a friend's kitchen where I had collected the culture, and poured it over the tea the moment I got home. Within a day the kombucha had started working quietly on the counter next to the kimchi jars, the two cultures doing their separate business in the same warm corner of the kitchen.

By Sunday evening, both projects were underway, the kimchi souring in its jar and the kombucha souring in its own, and I felt the particular satisfaction of a weekend that produced something rather than merely passing. I drove the leftover jars back to my friend's house that same weekend, the car once again smelling of pickles, and promised that next time the kimchi and kombucha would happen on separate weekends, a promise I already suspect I will not keep. The car keys stayed on the kitchen counter the whole time after that, since neither jar needed another trip anywhere.

articles.title: From Seed to Sauce: A Year of Growing Tomatoes
articles.gist: A personal essay following a year of growing tomatoes, saving seeds, feeding the compost heap, and keeping bees on the side.
articles.text:
Growing tomatoes properly starts long before the weather turns warm, and every year I begin in the same way, sorting saved seeds from last year's best tomatoes on a cold morning in late winter. Seed saving has become as much a part of growing tomatoes for me as the planting itself, because the seeds from a plant that thrived in my particular soil and my particular morning light tend to do better the following year than anything bought new.

Compost is the other half of the story. I feed the compost heap all year with kitchen scraps and spent plants, and by spring the compost is dark and crumbly enough to dig generously into the beds where the tomatoes will go. Tomatoes are famously greedy feeders, and a heap of good compost does more for a strong crop of tomatoes than any bottled fertiliser I have tried. Every morning through summer I check both the tomatoes and the compost, since one depends entirely on the other.

I took up beekeeping two summers ago, largely because a friend convinced me that beekeeping would improve pollination for the tomatoes and the beans alike, and I have kept at beekeeping since, more for the company of the hive than for any measurable effect on the tomatoes. Checking the bees most mornings has become part of the same round as checking the compost heap and inspecting the tomatoes for blight, three habits that now share the same quiet hour before the day properly starts.

By late summer, the seed saving begins again: I choose the best tomatoes from the healthiest plants, scoop the seeds into a jar, and leave them to ferment briefly before drying them for next year. It is a small, closed loop, tomatoes to seed saving to compost to beekeeping and back to tomatoes, repeated every morning across a whole growing year, and it is the closest thing I have to a proper agricultural education, learned entirely in a back garden.

articles.title: Pruning and Training Tomatoes in Raised Beds
articles.gist: A how-to guide on pruning tomato vines grown in raised beds and why soil health underpins the whole method.
articles.text:
Tomatoes grown in raised beds behave differently from tomatoes grown straight in the ground, mostly because raised beds warm up faster in spring and drain more freely after rain, both of which change how aggressively you need to prune. I grow all my tomatoes in raised beds now, and the biggest lesson has been that soil health inside a raised bed can decline faster than in open ground if you are not deliberately maintaining it.

Pruning tomatoes in raised beds starts with removing the side shoots, the small stems that appear in the join between the main stalk and each leaf branch. Left alone, these side shoots turn a single tomato plant into a sprawling thicket that raised beds, with their limited width, simply cannot support. My friend, who also uses raised beds, prunes far more aggressively than I do, and her tomatoes are smaller in number but noticeably healthier for it, a trade she puts down entirely to soil health rather than technique.

Soil health in a raised bed depends heavily on what you add back each year, since raised beds do not have the same reserve of surrounding soil to draw nutrients from. I top up my raised beds with mulch every spring specifically to protect soil health, because tomatoes pull hard on nitrogen and potassium across a full season. Without that yearly addition, soil health in a raised bed can visibly worsen by the third or fourth year of growing tomatoes in the same spot.

Training the vines upward, rather than letting them sprawl, is the other half of managing tomatoes in raised beds well. I tie the main stem to a cane as it grows, checking most days and again after my friend's visits, since a chat over the fence usually turns into an inspection of both raised beds at once. Between careful pruning and attention to soil health, tomatoes in raised beds have become the most reliable crop in the whole garden, outperforming anything I grew before raised beds existed here.

articles.title: Community Garden Reports Bumper Tomato Harvest
articles.gist: A news-style report on a community garden's tomato harvest, its compost programme and a seed saving swap.
articles.text:
The community garden on Elm Street reported its largest tomato harvest in six years this week, with volunteers crediting a new compost programme introduced last spring. Organisers say the tomatoes grown this season, several varieties across twelve beds, benefited directly from compost produced on site rather than trucked in, cutting costs while improving yields of tomatoes across every plot.

Volunteer coordinator Priya Shah said the compost system, which processes kitchen waste donated by residents over each weekend, has transformed the soil in beds that previously struggled to support tomatoes at all. "We used to buy compost every year," Shah said. "Now the compost comes from the neighbourhood itself, and the tomatoes this year are proof it works." Bins for the compost programme sit near the entrance, and volunteers empty each box of scraps into the main compost heap most weekends. Turnout for the harvest and the swap always peaks on weekends, when volunteers who work weekdays finally have time to visit the garden, and the compost bins are checked most weekends by a rotating team of three volunteers. Next year's planning meeting is already set for a weekend in late winter, well before the next tomato season begins.

Alongside the tomato harvest, the garden held its annual seed saving swap on Saturday, drawing residents from across the area with jars and envelopes of saved seeds. Seed saving has become a quiet tradition at the garden, with several long-time volunteers bringing tomato seeds passed down from plants grown in the same beds for a decade. One volunteer arrived by car with an entire box of labelled envelopes, distributing seed saving packets to newcomers who had never grown tomatoes before. Each box is labelled by household, so volunteers can track whose scraps are going into the heap, and by the end of the day every box at the swap table had been picked over at least once.

Shah said the seed saving swap and the compost programme are now treated as a single project rather than two separate ones, since seeds saved from tomatoes grown in the community's own compost tend to perform best in the same soil the following year. The garden plans to expand both the compost bins and the seed saving swap next year, with a second box for compost donations expected to arrive before the next tomato season begins.

articles.title: Building Raised Beds Before the Spring Rush
articles.gist: A how-to guide on building raised beds in late winter, with an aside on the beekeeping that will follow once beds are settled.
articles.text:
Late winter is the best time to build raised beds, before the ground softens and before the spring rush of seedlings demands a place to go. I built three new raised beds last month, working most days for a fortnight, and the process taught me more about soil health than any book on the subject had managed. Loading the timber for the raised beds had taken two trips in the car that morning, the boot barely closing around the last few planks.

The first lesson is that raised beds are only as good as what goes inside them. I filled mine with a mix of topsoil, aged manure and last year's leaf mould, layered deliberately to protect soil health from the very first planting. Raised beds built on poor filler soil look fine for a season but decline quickly, and soil health in a badly filled bed can undo years of careful gardening above ground.

Once the raised beds were framed and filled, I turned to a project I had been putting off: beekeeping. A hive sits at the far end of the plot now, close enough to the raised beds that the bees can reach the blossoms within hours of waking, but far enough that nobody working the beds gets in the flight path. Beekeeping alongside raised beds has an obvious logic to it, since the bees improve pollination for whatever ends up growing in the beds, and I check the hive most days on the same walk that takes me past the beds themselves.

A passer-by who drove past while I was finishing the last of the raised beds stopped his car to ask whether I was taking up beekeeping as well as gardening. He had the car radio on loud enough that I could hear it from the beds, and he left the car running at the kerb the whole time we talked. By the time the car was finally empty of his shopping and he drove off, the raised beds were nearly finished, and I admitted that soil health had led me there almost by accident. Good raised beds need good soil health, good soil health benefits from what a working hive brings to the wider garden, and beekeeping, once I started, turned out to belong far more naturally beside raised beds than I had expected when I first began building them this winter.

By the time spring arrives, the raised beds will have settled, the soil health will have evened out, and the beekeeping will already be established well before the first seedlings go in, which is exactly the order I would recommend to anyone building raised beds from scratch.

articles.title: Keeping the Compost Heap Working Through Winter
articles.gist: An essay on maintaining an active compost heap and healthy soil through the cold months, feeding next year's raised beds.
articles.text:
Compost does not stop over winter, though it slows enough that most gardeners forget about it until spring reminds them. I turn my compost heap most days through the cold months, not because it needs daily attention but because the walk past it has become a habit I would otherwise miss, and a heap left untouched for weeks can quietly lose the soil health it was building.

A neighbour of mine gave up on compost a few winters ago, convinced that cold weather made the whole effort pointless, but compost simply needs a different kind of care in winter rather than none at all. Insulating the heap with straw, and keeping a lid or a box over the top to stop it getting waterlogged, protects the compost and the soil health it eventually delivers to the raised beds each spring. My neighbour has since started again, having watched my own compost heap keep working steadily through two full winters. My neighbour and I compare notes over the fence most weeks, trading tips about heap temperature, and it was my neighbour, in fact, who first showed me how to layer straw into a heap properly.

Soil health is really the whole point of the exercise, since compost on its own is only useful for what it does to the ground it eventually joins. I dig last year's compost into the raised beds every February specifically to protect soil health before the growing season properly starts, and the difference between a bed that has had compost and one that has not becomes obvious by midsummer. Raised beds fed well in winter carry that soil health advantage through an entire season of tomatoes and beans.

By the time the cold months end, the compost heap has usually shrunk to a third of its autumn size, transformed into the dark material that will go straight into the raised beds. My neighbour now keeps her own box beside the heap for kitchen scraps, checking it most days the way I do, and between the two of us the compost, and the soil health it protects, has become a small shared winter project rather than a solitary one.

articles.title: A Practical Guide to Saving Seeds
articles.gist: A how-to guide on saving seeds from this year's tomatoes and other vegetables to protect soil health and reduce yearly costs.
articles.text:
Seed saving is one of those gardening skills that sounds intimidating until you actually try it, and the truth is that most tomatoes make seed saving almost effortless. I choose the healthiest tomatoes from the strongest plants each year, scoop the pulp and seeds into a jar, and leave the mixture to ferment for a few days before rinsing and drying, a method that has served my seed saving habit for a decade.

Seed saving from tomatoes works because the fermentation step removes the gel coating that would otherwise inhibit germination, so a little patience at this stage pays off the following spring. I keep the drying seeds on a labelled box on the windowsill, checking them most days until they are fully dry and ready to store, at which point the seed saving process is essentially complete for another year. A second box, smaller and lined with paper towel, holds whatever is still drying at any given time.

Beyond tomatoes, seed saving depends heavily on soil health, since a plant grown in poor soil produces weaker seeds even if the fruit looks fine. I only save seeds from beds where the soil health has been maintained with mulch and rotation, because seed saving from a struggling plant tends to pass that weakness forward. Good soil health, in other words, is really the first step of seed saving, long before any seed is actually collected.

I store the finished seed saving envelopes in an old shoe box in a cool cupboard, each one labelled with the tomatoes variety and the year, and I drove a box of duplicates to a friend last month so she could start her own seed saving habit. By the end of the season I usually need a third box just for the overflow. Seed saving costs nothing beyond a little attention across a season, and once the soil health in your beds is reliable, tomatoes especially will reward the seed saving habit with plants that seem to understand your garden a little better every single year.

articles.title: Keeping Bees Alongside the Vegetable Beds
articles.gist: An essay on taking up beekeeping at an allotment and folding the honey harvest into seasonal cooking, with soil health as an unexpected benefit.
articles.text:
I took up beekeeping on the allotment three summers ago, mostly on a neighbour's suggestion, and it has since become the part of the plot I check first most mornings, before the vegetables and before the hive tools are even put away. That same neighbour still calls the hive 'her bees' half-jokingly, since she was the one who talked me into it. Beekeeping asks for a different kind of attention than growing does, quieter and more careful, but it rewards a morning visit with a hum that tells you within seconds whether the hive is thriving.

The honey harvest has become its own small ritual of seasonal cooking, arriving each year just as the last of the summer vegetables are finishing and the first of the seasonal cooking for autumn begins. I fold the honey from beekeeping into whatever seasonal cooking the month calls for, drizzled over roasted autumn vegetables or stirred into a pot of something slow on a cold morning, and it tastes distinctly of this particular allotment in a way no shop honey ever has.

What surprised me most about beekeeping was its effect on soil health, indirectly but noticeably, since better pollination has meant heavier fruit set and more plant matter returning to the ground each year. Beekeeping is not something I took up for soil health reasons, but the connection has become obvious over three summers of watching the beds either side of the hive outperform the ones further away. My neighbour, who first pushed me towards beekeeping, now credits the bees for improvements in soil health she cannot otherwise explain. Another neighbour two doors down has since asked about starting a hive of her own, and I gave that neighbour a jar of the first honey harvest as a thank-you for putting up with the bees drifting over her fence.

On a quiet morning I will often sit near the hive with tea, watching the bees leave and return, and think about how naturally beekeeping has folded into both seasonal cooking and the quieter business of soil health. The honey itself, spooned into seasonal cooking through autumn and winter, is only the most obvious gift; the more lasting one is a garden that beekeeping has made steadily better every single morning since I started.
